title: Gradient-boosted trees distinguish historical autism diagnostic categories
summary: Gradient-boosted trees classified historical DSM-IV autism categories using assessment scores, demographics and comorbidities. In a person-separated SPARK test set, the multiclass model correctly classified 80.5% of individuals; 12.6% were assigned a different autism-spectrum category. This retrospective result does not establish screening performance under current DSM-5 criteria.

source_review.scope: Read actual primary dataset/reference definition, person-separated partition, gradient-boosted model/tuning Methods, input table, classification Results and limitations. Supplementary ABIDE tables were not independently inspected; their outcomes are not represented as external validation. Exact primary identity/date and fresh primary PubMed correction/retraction relationships checked.

evidence.tested: SPARK supplied 36,965 individuals, split 80:20 without person overlap; fivefold training-only grid search optimized gradient-boosted trees. The multiclass model correctly classified 5,951 of 7,393 test individuals (80.5%), with 933 assigned a different autism-spectrum category. Separate one-versus-reference models yielded AUROCs 0.863–0.980. ABIDE supported a separately developed model, not external testing of the SPARK model.
evidence.unknown: Historical professional DSM-IV diagnoses were the reference; absence of diagnostic codes defined non-spectrum controls. Assessment inputs overlap with information used in diagnostic evaluation, limiting independent screening interpretation. SPARK and ABIDE models used different inputs and were fitted separately. No prospective workflow, patient benefit or current DSM-5 diagnostic validation was established; PDD-NOS positive predictive value was low.
evidence.ai_role: Gradient-boosted trees learned associations between clinical/assessment features and recorded diagnostic categories, then classified unseen individuals from the same retrospective dataset.
